Abstract - Rice agriculture in Indonesia faces climate variability and limited access to timely field information. This paper presents Matani, a padi-only mobile decision support application for inspecting dated Sentinel-2 Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), short-wave-infrared-derived Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI), weather context, and field notes over time. Matani presents raw observations and explicit fixture, prototype, measured, or unavailable states; it does not classify crop health, diagnose disease or stress, predict yield, or synthesize missing observations. The advisor-approved retrospective study covered one verified 0.157-ha padi field in Teluknaga, Banten, from 1 July 2025 to 1 July 2026. Of 86 intersecting acquisitions, 32 met the provisional floors of at least nine valid NDVI pixels and three valid NDMI pixels, while 54 were rejected. The dry-labelled period had 30 passing acquisitions out of 60 and at least one passing observation in every dry month, supporting a monthly dry-season cadence for this site. The wet-labelled period had two passing acquisitions out of 26, with none in December through February, so no wet-season cadence is defensible. These findings are site-specific and do not establish national cadence or agronomic accuracy. The repository also contains a locally verified exact-polygon measurement path with native 10 m NDVI and 20 m NDMI processing, matched source provenance, quality decisions, typed persistence, and mobile read/retry behavior. The public backend health endpoint is reachable, but hosted database migration, server-only worker configuration, authenticated device persistence, user acceptance testing, and field validation remain unverified.
Keywords - rice field monitoring, time series, NDVI, NDMI, Sentinel-2, remote sensing, weather context, decision support system, measurement provenance
I. INTRODUCTION

Indonesia is an agrarian country with a population of more than 270 million people and a continuing need to maintain national food security. Agriculture, forestry, and fishing contributed approximately 12.5% of Indonesia's gross domestic product in 2023, w

hile employment in agriculture accounted for about 28.8% of total employment [1], [2]. Rice (Oryza sativa L.) remains the country's primary staple crop. According to BPS-Statistics Indonesia, Indonesia's paddy harvested area in 2023 reached about 10.20 mil
lion hectares, producing approximately 53.63 million tons of dry unhusked paddy [3].
Despite its importance, rice farming in Indonesia still faces several operational challenges. Climate variability has made rainfall patterns and temperature conditions les

s predictable, affecting irrigation availability and increasing exposure to drought, excessive rainfall, heat stress, and inundation. At the same time, many farmers have limited access to accurate and location-specific information about crop condition, wat
er stress, and local weather risk. As a result, field management decisions are often based on experience alone rather than timely data.
Remote sensing offers a practical way to observe rice fields at broad spatial coverage without requiring continuous grou
nd measurement. Multispectral satellite data can be processed into vegetation and moisture indices
that describe crop greenness, canopy development, and water-related stress. NDVI is widely used to monitor vegetation vigor, while SWIR-based indicators, suc

h as moisture-related indices derived from near-infrared and SWIR bands, can provide additional information related to crop water content and soil moisture conditions [4], [5]. When combined with weather data, these indicators can support early identificat
ion of field-level risk patterns.

This study presents Matani as a padi-only mobile decision support prototype for inspecting explicitly state-labeled satellite-index, weather, and field-note observations over time. The product displays dated raw NDVI/NDMI

values when available and an explicit unavailable state otherwise. It does not classify crop health, diagnose disease or stress, predict yield, or synthesize missing observations. The paper-defined GROW workflow frames Gathering available inputs, Recognizi

ng observable changes without causal interpretation, Offering educational context or optional descriptive summaries, and Warning through transparent weather-context indicators; thesis-target monitoring depends on the quality-gated measurement pipeline.

The long-term goal of Matani is to support a more resilient rice-farming workflow by making field context and uncertainty easier to inspect. Any contribution to improved farm management, poverty reduction, or food security remains a future i
mpact hypothesis; those outcomes were not evaluated in this study.
II. LITERATURE REVIEW
A. NDVI, SWIR, and Remote Sensing for Rice
Remote sensing has been widely used for rice field mapping, phenology monitoring, and crop condition assessment. Zhao et al.

reviewed satellite-based rice mapping methods and highlighted the importance of multi-temporal optical, microwave, and multisource remote sensing approaches for paddy rice monitoring [4]. Kuenzer and Knauer also discussed remote sensing methods for rice c
rop areas, showing that vegetation indices and temporal image patterns are central to rice field analysis [6].
NDVI is one of the most established vegetation indices for describing crop greenness, canopy development, and biomass-related variation. Guan et

al. demonstrated that high-resolution UAV-derived NDVI was related to fertilizer application levels and yield variation in rice and wheat fields [7]. Jiang et al. further showed that UAV operation parameters, including flight altitude and acquisition timin
g, influence NDVI quality in paddy rice fields [8]. Although UAV imagery can provide very high
spatial resolution, its limited coverage and operational cost make it less suitable as the only monitoring layer for scattered smallholder fields.
Satellite-deri

ved NDVI is also useful for broader-scale monitoring. Huang et al. showed that multi-temporal NDVI derived from satellite data can support rice yield trend analysis and reflect seasonal vegetation dynamics [9]. However, NDVI primarily captures structural v

egetation conditions and may be less sensitive to early water stress or moisture variation. For this reason, SWIR-based indicators are relevant because SWIR reflectance is commonly used in vegetation water-content and soil-moisture assessment. Recent revie

ws of Sentinel-based soil moisture assessment show that Sentinel-1 radar data and Sentinel-2 multispectral indices, including moisture-related indices such as NDMI, are frequently integrated with machine learning to improve agricultural water monitoring [5

These studies indicate that NDVI is appropriate for structural crop condition monitoring, while SWIR-derived moisture indicators can complement NDVI by adding water-stress information. Therefore, a mobile decision support system for rice farming should
avoid relying on a single index and should instead combine vegetation, moisture, and weather indicators in a form that is understandable for farmers.
B. Machine Learning for Rice Monitoring and Decision Support
Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL)

techniques have been widely applied to rice yield estimation and crop monitoring using satellite and multi-source data. Cao et al. integrated satellite imagery, weather variables, and management data to predict rice yield across large regions in China [10]

. Son et al. developed ML models using time-series MODIS NDVI data for rice yield prediction in Taiwan [11]. Jeong et al. combined crop growth models and deep learning to predict rice yield at pixel scale using satellite data in South and North Korea [12].
Son et al. also used Sentinel-2 monthly image composites with ML algorithms for field-scale rice yield estimation [13].
Beyond yield estimation, ML has been used to classify rice production stages and analyze vegetation dynamics. Thorp and Drajat applied

deep learning with Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data to map paddy rice production stages across West Java, Indonesia, using extensive ground survey data [14]. Their study demonstrates the relevance of combining satellite data and machine learning for rice mon
itoring in the Indonesian context.

However, many yield-prediction and anomaly-detection studies depend on historical outcomes, detailed ground truth, and extensive calibration datasets. Such data are unavailable for the present Matani evaluation. Machine-l
earning-based crop-health inference, anomaly attribution, growth-stage classification, and risk prediction are therefore outside the implemented and evaluated scope.
C. Environmental Stress Monitoring and Rice Phenology
Vegetation indices can be used to de
tect abnormal growth patterns associated with environmental stress in paddy rice. Ryu et al. evaluated vegetation indices under elevated air temperature, heat stress, and herbicide damage,
showing that NDVI can represent structural crop development and hel

p detect abnormal growth conditions before the heading stage [15]. Their findings also indicate that different vegetation indices respond differently to structural, biochemical, and physiological stress conditions.
Further research by Ryu et al. showed tha

t NDVI and the Photochemical Reflectance Index (PRI) respond differently to heat stress damage in paddy rice at leaf and canopy scales [16]. These findings suggest that NDVI is useful for monitoring crop structure and development, while additional indices

may be required to capture early physiological stress. For scalable mobile applications using open-access satellite data, NDVI can serve as the primary structural indicator, while SWIR-derived moisture indicators and weather variables can improve the inter
pretation of stress risk.

Time-series inspection can add value because a single vegetation-index value does not describe temporal change. Matani's current detail surface reads dated legacy fixture/prototype NDVI and NDMI rows without generating replacement
dates or values and without interpreting their direction as improvement, deterioration, or diagnosis. Provenance-safe measured history remains dependent on the target persistence pipeline.
D. Weather-Based Risk Indicators
Rice cultivation is highly sensit

ive to climatic variability, particularly during critical growth periods. Short-term extreme events such as heatwaves, excessive rainfall, drought periods, and prolonged inundation can reduce yield and weaken crop condition even before severe visual damage
appears. Compound dry and wet extremes during the rice-growing season have been shown to increase the risk of rice yield loss more strongly than individual dry or wet extremes [17].
Climate risk indicators are therefore important for rice farming decision

support. Chou et al. analyzed extreme climate events in rice-growing regions and used indicators such as warm days, consecutive dry days, maximum five-day precipitation, and rice heat damage indices to describe climate-related risk [18]. Jiang et al. furt
her examined heat exposure risk for single-season rice, showing the relevance of disaster-event-based heat risk assessment for rice production [19].
In the current Matani prototype, weather retrieval provides precipitation and humidity inputs to a client-s

ide heuristic score, defined later in Section III.I. The score is a rule-based presentation-layer indicator, not a calibrated agronomic model. More complex indicators such as consecutive dry days, heatwave duration, or inundation risk remain future extensi
ons unless they are implemented, versioned, and validated.
E. Research Gap

Although previous studies have demonstrated the value of multispectral satellite data, vegetation indices, SWIR-derived moisture indicators, and machine learning for rice monitoring, several gaps remain in operational farmer-facing decision support systems

First, local sensor-based systems, such as Internet of Things (IoT) devices and ground-based sensors, can provide high-resolution field information, but their cost, maintenance requirements, data storage needs, and rural network limitations can reduce ad

option among smallholder farmers. A recent systematic review of IoT and AI in agriculture identified high infrastructure costs, limited interoperability, connectivity constraints, and unequal access as major barriers to implementation [20]. Low-cost remote
sensing approaches have been explored for smallholder agriculture, but UAV-based systems still face spatial coverage and operational constraints [21].
Second,

traditional monitoring methods based on manual field surveys require substantial time, labor, and financial resources, particularly for national-scale coverage across millions of hectares of rice fields[4]. Many ML-based yield prediction studies also requi

re extensive historical yield records and detailed ground truth data, which are not always available in smallholder farming contexts[10]. This creates a need for decision support approaches that can work with accessible satellite and weather data while sti
ll communicating uncertainty clearly.

Third, the operational integration of weather data, dated NDVI/NDMI observations, and field notes into a transparent mobile time series remains underdeveloped [5]. Many systems present weather separately, while remote-

sensing studies often require expert interpretation. There is a need for interfaces that expose observation dates, missingness, and provenance limits without converting index values into crop-health diagnoses.
Matani addresses this gap by combining dated N

DVI and SWIR-derived NDMI observations, weather context, field notes, and optional descriptive AI summaries within a mobile time-series interface. Health classification, diagnosis, anomaly attribution, and prediction remain outside the evaluated implementa
tion.
The measurement evaluation is guided by two active research questions; an independent raster-comparison question is retained only as optional future work:

RQ1: Within the approved padi study field in Teluknaga, Banten, what proportion of Sentinel-2 acquisitions produces quality-passing polygon-level NDVI and NDMI observations, and what monitoring cadence is defensible during the locally labelled wet and dry seasons?

Optional future work: How closely do pipeline-derived polygon statistics agree with independently derived raster zonal statistics for the same polygon, source product, acquisition time, bands, mask, and grid policy? This comparison is not an active thesis acceptance requirement.

RQ3: For the approved Teluknaga padi field, how many valid NDVI and NDMI pixels are available per acquisition under the provisional quality floors, and what measurement limitations arise from the field's size and Sentinel-2 spatial resolution?
III. METHODOLOGY
A. Research Design

This study employs a system-development and decision-support research approach to design Matani as a padi-only mobile application for rice-field time-series monitoring. The active measurement evaluation is a one-field, one-site retrospective case study over the advisor-approved Teluknaga padi boundary and its locally labelled wet and dry seasons. The application and research remain observation-first: Matani displays dated raw NDVI/NDMI values and explicit data states, but does not provide crop-health classes, diagnosis, exact yield prediction, or soil-fertility prediction. The provisional valid-pixel floors classify observations for this study only, while the client-side weather-context score remains author-defined and uncalibrated.
B. System Development Workflow

The development of Matani follows the paper-defined GROW workflow: (1) Gathering field boundaries, available satellite observations, weather, and field notes; (2) Recognizing dated values, quality states, and observable changes without causal or health interpretation; (3) Offering educational context and optional descriptive summaries; and (4) Warning through a transparent, uncalibrated weather-context indicator. Fig. 1 illustrates this workflow.
Fig. 1. The GROW decision support workflow: data gathering, pattern recognition, recommendation offering, and risk warning.
In this study, GROW is defined as an application-specific workflow

for the Matani decision support system. GROW stands for Gathering, Recognizing, Offering, and Warning. The workflow is designed based on the general concept of agricultural decision support systems, which collect and process agricultural data to support fa

rm decision-making through interpretation, recommendations, or predictions [22], [23]. It also reflects the importance of visual and user-centered interfaces in transforming agricultural data into information that farmers can understand and use [24], [25].

The GROW workflow begins with Gathering user-defined padi-field boundaries and retrieving weather plus explicitly state-labeled satellite inputs. Recognizing organizes dated values and observable changes without assigning crop-health meaning or causal diagnosis. Offering presents educational content and optional descriptive summaries. Warning presents heuristic weather context only with visible limitations. The exact-polygon measurement path is implemented and verified locally; its hosted database, worker configuration, and authenticated device delivery remain deployment gates.

E. Field Boundary Processing

Users define padi fields by drawing polygon boundaries in WGS84. The database derives a geography-based field area, while a centroid is used only for location-based weather retrieval. The current measurement implementation validates and hashes the stored exact polygon, projects it to a local UTM coordinate reference system, and processes native 10 m NDVI and 20 m NDMI grids without substituting a bounding box as the measurement geometry. Saving a valid field creates or reuses a durable measurement job; screen rendering does not trigger satellite acquisition. This behavior is locally verified, while hosted persistence and authenticated device delivery remain unverified.
F. Satellite Data Processing

The current measurement worker discovers one intersecting Sentinel-2 Level-2A acquisition and requests two exact-polygon Process responses so the native output grids are preserved: NDVI at 10 m from B04 and B08, and NDMI at 20 m from B08 and B11. Each raster response carries source metadata, and persistence is rejected unless both responses identify the same acquisition. A common display or analysis grid must not be described as creating new 10 m spatial detail in B11 [26].

Weather data are retrieved for the user's location or a selected field centroid through the backend's Open-Meteo route. Weather values provide temporal context for field observations. Provider failures are normalized into an unavailable r

The prototype translates average forecast precipitation and a representative humidity value into a client-side heuristic indicator. These inputs and weights demonstrate interface behavior; they are not a cali

I. Weather-Context Heuristic
The prototype employs a heuristic scoring model developed in this study to translate selected weather variables into simple risk levels for farmer-facing decision support. Pr

ecipitation and relative humidity are selected as inputs because rice cultivation is sensitive to water-related extremes, including insufficient rainfall, excessive rainfall, and wet atmospheric conditions that may increase field monitoring needs [17]-[19]
The heuristic prototype formula is defined as:
Risk Score = min(100, max(0, (Pavg × 4) + (H × 0.4)))
where Pavg is the average daily precipitation in millimeters over the forecast period, and H is the representative relative humidity value obtained from
current weather data when available. The coefficients 4 and 0.4 are heuristic weights defined in the prototype to emphasize precipitation as the dominant short-term water-
related risk factor, while humidity provides secondary modulation.
This score is not

adopted from an established agronomic risk model. It is an author-defined prototype indicator calculated in the mobile presentation layer and is not calibrated against local field observations. Its value is therefore shown as a heuristic score rather than
a probability of crop loss.

J. Recommendation Generation

Matani provides static educational content and an optional Gemini-based summarization service. The service receives an explicit fixture, prototype, measured, or unavailable state with each NDVI/NDMI input and may summarize that state, field area, index val

ues, and weather context into plain-language text. It is not a classifier, sensor, measurement source, research label, or ground truth. The service prompt forbids converting fixture/prototype input into measurements or diagnoses and forbids chemical-applic
ation instructions; generated text remains optional, requires field verification, and must not be interpreted as validated agronomic advice.
K. Prototype Testing and Evaluation

Evaluation separates software behavior from measurement validity so that a successful interface, test, or API response is never treated as proof of agronomic accuracy. On 30 August 2026, an empty local database migration and 26 database assertions passed together with the Python research fixture suite. On 31 August 2026, scoped lint, root and backend type checks, nine root tests, and 36 backend tests passed again. The public backend health endpoint returned JSON with HTTP 200, and a protected weather request without a token failed closed with HTTP 401. The Python research suite could not be rerun on the 31 August workstation because Python 3 was unavailable. User acceptance testing and field validation have not been completed.
1) Functional and Security Verification: Automated checks c
over required artifact boundaries, protected provider routes, request limits, provider-contract behavior, and research request construction. These tests verify
software behavior and do not convert fixtures or provider responses into field measurements.

API and Research-Path Verification: Deterministic tests exercise response schema, band arithmetic, masking, retry behavior, exact-polygon requests, and accounting. Explicit live CDSE runs are bounded and reported separately from ordinary verification.

3) Conceptual Plausibility: NDVI/NDMI behavior may be compared cautiously with rice phenology literature [4], [9]. Such comparison is contextual only and cannot replace field-level ground truth. Independent raster comparison remains a useful optional extension, but it is outside the active thesis acceptance scope.

4) User Acceptance Testing: A future qualitative evaluation must assess whether users understand dates, raw index values, data-state labels, unavailable outcomes, weather-context caveats, and optional descriptive summaries. It will evaluate usability and c
omprehension rather than agronomic accuracy.

5) Measurement Limitations: The approved study contains one 0.157-ha Teluknaga field and therefore cannot establish a universal minimum field area, nationally representative cadence, or agronomic validity. The nine-NDVI/three-NDMI floors are provisional operational rules rather than universally validated reliability thresholds. The public summary supports acquisition-level pass/reject counts but does not justify inventing an unreported full distribution of pixel counts. The exact-polygon measurement path is locally verified, yet hosted migration, worker credentials, authenticated device persistence/read, ground truth, and completed user acceptance testing remain open.

L. Limitations

Both product and thesis scope are restricted to padi. The approved retrospective evidence covers one 0.157-ha Teluknaga field, uses provisional nine-NDVI/three-NDMI valid-pixel floors, and supports only the advisor-reviewed site-specific cadence statement: monthly in the locally labelled dry period and no defensible cadence in the wet period. The local application path includes exact-polygon processing, versioned masking, matched source provenance, typed persistence, owner-scoped access, and explicit unavailable outcomes. The stable public backend alias is reachable and protected routes fail closed, but hosted measurement migration, server-only worker credentials, authenticated physical-device persistence/read, field-level ground truth, completed user acceptance testing, and production notifications remain unverified.

M. Three-Layer System Architecture
Matani has an Expo mobile presentation layer, an Express integration layer, Supabase persisten

ce, external providers, and a separate research acquisition workspace. Satellite, weather, and Gemini requests cross the authenticated backend boundary; mapping, place search, and display-only media do not enter the measurement path.

The padi-only mobile application provides account access, polygon drawing, an explicit save/retry measurement request, dated NDVI/NDMI time-series display, backend-mediated Open-Meteo weather information, an uncalibrated client-side weather-context indicator, optional descriptive AI summaries, field notes, and explicit queued, rejected, unavailable, and query-failure states. It does not classify crop health, diagnose field conditions, synthesize missing observations, or deliver production alerts. The measured-history interface is implemented locally, while populated hosted history is not yet verified.

The Express backend exposes protected weather, legacy satellite, optional AI, and measurement routes. The measurement route verifies a Supabase bearer token, checks field ownership and request bounds, then invokes the controlled worker outside UI rendering. The stable Vercel production alias returned JSON with HTTP 200 at its health endpoint on 31 August 2026, and a protected weather request without a token returned HTTP 401. These checks establish reachability and fail-closed authentication only; they do not establish that hosted measurement credentials or persistence are configured.

Supabase stores identity, exact field polygons, notes, durable measurement jobs, typed measurements, per-index statistics, and a security-invoker observation view through versioned migrations and owner-scoped row-level security. Clean local application and database assertions pass, but the measurement migration is not confirmed on hosted Supabase. CDSE endpoint defaults and Open-Meteo-only weather routing are active, while Gemini remains optional presentation support. Server-only Supabase administration and CDSE configuration on the public deployment, plus an authenticated device save-to-read flow, remain unverified.
IV. RESULTS
A. Engineering Verification

The locally verified repository state separates software assurance from measurement evidence. On 30 August 2026, the complete verification record included an empty-database migration, 26 database assertions, the Python research fixture suite, lint, type checks, and application/backend tests. On 31 August, lint, root/backend type checks, nine root tests, and 36 backend tests passed again; the Python suite could not be rerun because Python 3 was unavailable. The public backend health endpoint returned JSON with HTTP 200 and a protected route without a token returned HTTP 401. These results establish the audited software and authentication behavior only; they do not establish scientific validity, hosted measurement persistence, physical-device success, or user acceptance.
B. Approved Teluknaga Feasibility Study

The advisor-approved private study covered one verified 0.157-ha padi field in Teluknaga, Banten, from 1 July 2025 to 1 July 2026. The bounded run completed 12 field-months, 48 successful provider operations in 48 attempts, and consumed approximately 4.203 processing units. It returned 86 intersecting acquisitions: 32 passed the provisional floors of at least nine valid NDVI pixels and three valid NDMI pixels, while 54 were rejected. During locally labelled dry months, 30 of 60 acquisitions passed and every dry month had at least two passing observations. During wet months, two of 26 passed; December, January, and February had none, while March had two. The advisor-reviewed interpretation is monthly cadence for the dry period and no defensible cadence for the wet period, scoped only to this Teluknaga field.
C. Locally Implemented Measurement Path

The repository implements a durable exact-polygon measurement path with authenticated jobs, Catalog discovery, separate native-grid NDVI and NDMI Process responses, strict source-identity matching, versioned quality rules, typed provenance persistence, owner isolation, and mobile request/read/retry behavior. A bounded provider-adapter smoke over the approved polygon selected one July 2026 acquisition and matched one source product; all 23 NDVI pixels and all six NDMI pixels in that response were valid, and the operation consumed approximately 0.05 processing units across three first-attempt provider calls. This is a provider-adapter result, not proof of hosted persistence, a universal pixel rule, or scientific validity.
V. DISCUSSION
A. Answer to RQ1

For the approved Teluknaga field, 32 of 86 acquisitions, or 37.2%, passed both provisional valid-pixel floors. The dry-labelled period passed 30 of 60 acquisitions and included usable observations in every dry month, supporting a monthly dry-season cadence for this site. The wet-labelled period passed only two of 26 acquisitions and had no passing observation in December through February; no wet-season cadence is therefore defensible. This answer is site- and season-label-specific and must not be generalized nationally.
B. Answer to RQ3

The approved field is 0.157 ha. Thirty-two acquisitions contained at least nine valid 10 m NDVI pixels and at least three valid 20 m NDMI pixels; 54 failed one or both provisional floors. This outcome shows that the coarser NDMI grid is a distinct constraint and that acquisition-level counts must remain separate by index. The retained public summary does not provide a complete numeric pixel-count distribution for all 86 acquisitions, so no median, range, or universal minimum-area relationship is claimed. The separate July 2026 adapter smoke yielded 23 valid NDVI pixels and six valid NDMI pixels for one selected acquisition, but that single operation cannot establish a general rule.
C. Status of Optional Independent Comparison

Independent raster-derived comparison is excluded from the active thesis acceptance scope and retained only as optional future work. The current same-response source metadata and strict cross-response identity matching protect provenance within the implemented provider path, but they are not an independent accuracy assessment.
D. Product and Deployment Implication

The application and worker are implemented and verified locally, and the stable public backend alias is reachable. However, the hosted measurement migration, server-only worker configuration, and authenticated physical-device save-to-persist-to-read flow have not been verified. A newly created field may therefore remain empty in the hosted application. Only a provenance-complete row written through the controlled completion path may be presented as measured; research outputs and legacy rows are not promoted.
VI. CONCLUSION AND REMAINING WORK

Matani now has a padi-only mobile DSS implementation for requesting and inspecting dated, quality-gated NDVI/NDMI observations while keeping fixture, prototype, measured, rejected, and unavailable semantics explicit. The approved one-field Teluknaga study found that 32 of 86 acquisitions passed the provisional nine-NDVI/three-NDMI pixel floors. Its complete dry-month pattern supports monthly cadence for the locally labelled dry period, while only two passing wet acquisitions support no defensible wet-season cadence. These results are site-specific and do not establish national cadence, universal thresholds, crop-health diagnosis, or agronomic accuracy. The exact-polygon measurement worker, typed persistence, source matching, and mobile flow are locally verified, and the public backend is reachable, but hosted migration, worker configuration, authenticated device persistence, field validation, user acceptance testing, and final thesis-team/advisor approval remain necessary.
